props.title: The Long Arm
props.initialSlug: London cops track clever thief using new forensics

sections.content: **The Long Arm (1956)** (1956) stands as a pivotal British police procedural that helped establish conventions still used in crime thrillers today. Director Charles Frend crafted a gritty, realistic portrait of London police work that influenced later classics like The Blue Lamp (1950) and Odds Against Tomorrow (1959). Jack Hawkins delivers a commanding performance as Detective Inspector Tom Halliday, bringing gravitas to the methodical investigation style that would later influence characters in films like Z (1969) and **The French Connection** (1971).

sections.content: The film's innovative focus on forensic detail and procedural accuracy marked a significant shift from the more sensationalized crime pictures of the era. Where Hollywood noir emphasized shadows and psychological drama, **The Long Arm** (1956) stripped away theatrical elements to show the unglamorous reality of police work. This documentary-style approach influenced European crime films like Le Samouraï (1967) and **The Day of the Jackal** (1973).

Most striking is how the film captures post-war London, using actual locations rather than studio sets. This verisimilitude became a hallmark of British crime cinema, seen later in Hell is a City (1960) and **The Criminal** (1960). The film's attention to technological advancement in police work - featuring early forensic techniques and communications systems - set a template for how procedurals would handle evolving law enforcement methods. sections.content: The legacy of **The Long Arm** (1956) extends beyond its immediate era. Its influence can be seen in the development of British television police series and international crime films that emphasize realistic investigative techniques. The film's measured pacing and focus on the minutiae of detective work created a blueprint followed by later works like **Serpico** (1973) and **The French Connection** (1971), which similarly emphasized the grinding nature of real police work over sensationalized action.
